newsitem.title: USA: FERC rejects Calif. pricing plan for Bonneville.
newsitem.headline: FERC rejects Calif. pricing plan for Bonneville.

text.p: The U.S. Federal Energy Regulatory Commission on Wednesday rejected a plan by California's three major electric utilities to offset the potential for Bonneville Power Administration (BPA) to dominate an open Californian power market.

At the same time, the commission approved the utilities' proposal for the California independent system operator to plan expansions and other changes on the power grid, and approved a proposal for the operator to charge an access fee at times when transmission lines are congested.
The rulings were part of the commission's ongoing review of California's plan to allow all electricity consumers in the state to choose their power suppliers from January 1, 1998.

The commission rejected the proposed pricing rule aimed at limiting Bonneville's market strength because the U.S. power agency had submitted a plan to offer equal access on its transmission lines to all power producers, just as investor-owned utilities were required to do.
"Bonneville has met the commission's standards for comparability (of service) and open access, and they must be allowed to participate in this market," said Commissioner William Massey.

To give itself enough time to complete its review before January 1, the FERC set a deadline of August 15 for Southern California Edison, San Diego Gas and Electric, and Pacific Gas and Electric to submit final revised plans for the independent system operator and power exchange.

The independent operator will be in charge of handling all power transmission to ensure that power deliveries remain reliable, while not allowing any transmission owners to limit competing power producers' access to the grid.

The commission said there would not be enough time before January to develop a system for trading transmission rights, as requested by some power market players, so the commission set a June 1998 deadline for the utilities to submit a plan to offer tradable transmission rights.

"Transmisssion rights are ... highly important to the development of a competitive market in California," said Massey, adding that the commission aimed to approve a system of resellable transmission rights by January 1999.
